summary: Defines SNMP management objects, using SMIv2, for monitoring and controlling devices that act as DLUR, the Dependent LU Requester, in IBM SNA networks. It helps network managers watch these gateways.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a set of dials and gauges for managers to check on a certain kind of old IBM network helper.

questions: how to manage sna dlur with snmp
what does the dlur mib monitor
does the dlur mib have read-write objects
subtitle: SNMP objects for watching an IBM SNA gateway that lets old dependent terminals work across an APPN network.

tldr.problem: APPN networks were built for independent logical units, but customers had large investments in dependent LU applications. Devices that run DLUR to support them needed a standard way to be monitored over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2232 defines a read-only SMIv2 MIB module with three groups of objects: node capabilities and default backup servers, the physical units the node serves, and the control sessions to dependent LU servers.
tldr.outcome: A network manager can see what a DLUR node supports, which PUs it serves and the state of its sessions to each DLUS. It cannot configure anything: the module has no read-write objects and no traps.

today: RFC 2232 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this unit lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2232 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) used by network management protocols in the Internet community. Its objects are for monitoring and controlling network devices that have DLUR (Dependent LU Requester) capabilities.

The SNMP Network Management Framework supplies the pieces this memo relies on: the SMI and related documents (RFC 1902, RFC 1903 and RFC 1904) that describe how objects are named and described. The module is written in SMIv2.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a list of things a manager can look at on one kind of IBM network gadget. It is written in the standard way so any management tool can read it.

sections.title: DLUR, DLUS and APPN
sections.content:
Dependent LU requester/server (DLUR/S) is an extension to APPN (Advanced Peer-to-Peer Networking). The base APPN architecture only carried data between independent logical units (LUs). The RFC notes that customers had an enormous investment in applications based on dependent LU types, and DLUR/S adds support for dependent LU sessions in an APPN network.

A dependent LU server (DLUS) is an APPN node that provides System Services Control Point (SSCP) services over the APPN network to remote secondary dependent LUs. It does this with SSCP-PU and SSCP-LU sessions whose flows are encapsulated on LU 6.2 session flows between the DLUS node and the DLUR node.

Those LU 6.2 control sessions are called a CPSVRMGR pipe, named after the mode used for the sessions. The APPN MIB in RFC 2155 covers management of APPN networks themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old computer programs only know how to talk if a boss machine guides them. The DLUR is a local helper that fetches that guidance from the boss over a newer network, using a private pipe.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
Although DLUR extends APPN, the DLUR MIB relies very little on the APPN MIB. Two links exist: dlurNodeCpName has the same value as appnNodeCpName in the APPN MIB, and if dlurPuLsName equals appnLsName the two objects refer to the same link station.

The module has three collections of objects:

  • dlurNodeInfo: the capabilities and architecture options of the implementation, plus default primary and backup DLUSs.
  • dlurPuInfo: the physical units (PUs) the APPN node supports with DLUR.
  • dlurDlusInfo: the control sessions with DLUSs.

The module does not manage DLUSs, configure DLUR nodes, change the state of the control session to the DLUS, or show the dependent LUs the node supports. It also defines no traps.
sections.plainLanguage: The information is sorted into three drawers: one about the helper itself, one about the devices it helps, and one about the pipes to the boss machines.

sections.title: Node Capabilities and Backup Servers
sections.content:
The dlurNodeCapabilities objects describe what this DLUR implementation can do. dlurReleaseLevel is a two-character string: the one-byte value encoded in the DLUR/DLUS Capabilities control vector (CV 51) is shown as two displayable characters, so X'01' appears as 01.

dlurAnsSupport reports Automatic Network Shutdown capability, either continueOrStop or stopOnly. With ANS equal to continue, the DLUR node keeps LU-LU sessions active even if the SSCP-PU and SSCP-LU control sessions are interrupted. With stop, those LU-LU sessions are interrupted too.

Other objects say whether the node supports CPSVRMGR sessions that cross NetId boundaries, forwarding of Network Name control vectors, and nondisruptive deactivation of DLUR-DLUS sessions. There is also a default primary DLUS name and dlurDefaultDefBackupDlusTable, an ordered list of default backup DLUSs indexed from 1, where 1 is the most preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: These gauges tell you what the helper machine is able to do, and who its first-choice and spare boss machines are, in order.

sections.title: Served PUs and Their Status
sections.content:
dlurPuTable has one entry for each PU the node serves, indexed by the locally administered PU name (1 to 17 characters). An entry shows the name the SSCP supplied (or a zero-length string if none), the PU status, the ANS setting configured for that PU, whether the PU is internal or downstream, and the link station name for downstream PUs.

dlurPuStatus has nine values, from reset through pendActpu and active to pendInopActpu. Each pending state names what the DLUR is waiting for, such as a response from the DLUS to a Request ACTPU or a DACTPU response from the PU.

Each PU can have its own defined primary DLUS and its own ranked backup list in dlurPuDefBackupDlusTable. A PU with no entries there falls back to the node-wide default backup list, and a PU with no primary of its own uses the global default primary.
sections.plainLanguage: For each device the helper looks after, there is a light showing where it is in getting started, plus a note of which boss machine it should call first and which are the spares.

sections.title: Control Sessions to the DLUS
sections.content:
A DLUR uses a pair of CPSVRMGR sessions to talk to a DLUS, called the contention-winner and contention-loser sessions. For status purposes the MIB combines them into one value for the requester/server connection, in dlurDlusTable (indexed by DLUS name) and in dlurPuDlusSessnStatus for a PU's active DLUS.

The combined value is reset (1), pendingActive (2), active (3) or pendingInactive (4). It is active only when both sessions are active. It is pendingActive if either is pending active, and pendingInactive if either is pending inactive, with the pendingActive test made first. Anything else is reset.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two phone lines to each boss machine. The single light says green only when both lines are up, and shows amber if either one is still connecting or hanging up.

sections.title: Compliance
sections.content: The module is identified as dlurMIB, placed at { snanauMIB 5 }. Its single compliance statement, dlurCompliance, makes one group mandatory: dlurConfGroup. That group lists the node capability objects, the PU objects and the DLUS session status object.
sections.plainLanguage: To say you follow this list, you have to provide the one required set of gauges.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says MIBs are not themselves security risks when SNMP security works as intended: using one to view or change a system is a tool, not a threat. None of the read-only objects reports a password, user data or anything particularly sensitive, and there are no read-write objects in the DLUR MIB.

It does point out that some enterprises regard their network configuration, usage and performance information as corporate assets, and may want to restrict SNMP access to most of the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges do not show secrets, and nobody can change anything with them. Still, a company might not want strangers peeking at how its network is set up.

viz.caption: OBJECT GROUPS OF THE DLUR MIB

items.label: pendReqActpuRsp
items.desc: Pending a response from the DLUS to a Request ACTPU.

items.label: pendActpu
items.desc: Pending an ACTPU from the DLUS.

items.label: pendActpuRsp
items.desc: Pending an ACTPU response from the PU.

items.label: pendLinkact
items.desc: Pending activation of the link to a downstream PU.

items.label: pendDactpuRsp
items.desc: Pending a DACTPU response from the PU.

items.label: pendInop
items.desc: The CPSVRMGR pipe became inoperative while the DLUR was pending an ACTPU response from the PU.

items.label: pendInopActpu
items.desc: In pendInop, a pipe became active and a new ACTPU arrived before the earlier ACTPU was answered by the PU.

cells: Either session pending inactive (after the pendingActive test)
